sections.title: Phase 4: training on the eval itself, and what it did
sections.intro: Your idea: make the loss the eval metric, restricted to one stratum, and see what that does to every other stratum compared with optimising the average. First results are in, and the main one is that our models were not trained well enough for the question yet.

p: If we train a model on the eval metric itself, restricted to one slice of the data, what happens on every other slice? And is it better to optimise the average of all slices? We built the loss so that it IS the eval metric (computed on training points), then measured it on held-out points.

items.t: The eval metric and the loss
p: For each sequence the model gives two calls: host class and region. Each call can also be 'abstain'. Utility is +1 if right, -1 if wrong, 0 if it abstains, averaged over the two calls and over sequences. A wrong host call costs as much as a right one gains; that cost is a choice (lambda = 1) and we did not test other values. Where a threat triage tool would rather say 'I do not know' than be wrong, this metric rewards that.

The training loss is the negative of the same quantity, computed exactly from the model's probabilities (including the abstain option). It is the average that reinforcement learning with a verifiable reward estimates by sampling answers, without the sampling noise. We used the exact version because with 10 possible actions it is cheap and stable. It is reinforcement learning in expectation, not sampled roll-outs; multi-step agent RL is a separate thing we did not do.

p: A stratum is one virus in one region: influenza in Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania and South America, and rotavirus in Africa, Asia and Oceania (the other rotavirus regions have too few fully labelled sequences). Only sequences whose host AND region labels are both gold are used: 1,626 sequences.

list: Same encoder (ESM-2, 35M parameters), same 200 steps, same learning rates, same data pool for every fine-tuned condition. Three seeds each.
No early stopping and no hyperparameter search for any utility condition, so no condition gets to peek at other strata through a dev set.

The cross-entropy and probe models and the nearest-neighbour baseline cannot abstain, so they get a fair rule: abstain when the top probability is below a threshold picked on dev. The utility models learn their own abstaining.
Held-out evaluation = unseen countries + unseen host genera + 2022 and later. The blind split is evaluated once at the end.
Confidence intervals come from resampling the evaluation sequences within each stratum (500 resamples).

items.s: Tables update as runs land. The blind split is shown; no decision was based on it.
p: Utility is +1 right, -1 wrong, 0 abstain (higher is better, 0 is 'always abstain'). Distance tiers pool every non-training sequence, including the blind split. 'Held out' means unseen countries, unseen host genera, or 2022 and later. 'Blind' is a sealed split we looked at after the runs were done: it was not used to choose anything.
Where each model holds up: on sequences it has seen, or close to or far from what it has seen.

kids.t: Transfer matrix: train the utility phase on one stratum, evaluate on every other

items.t: What we found (verified numbers; details in the tables above)
list: 1. Utility loss from scratch fails, in two opposite ways. On the average or worst stratum the model learns to abstain (it answers 15 to 17% of held-out sequences). On one stratum alone it answers nearly everything but is right only 15 to 37% of the time.

2. A warm start fixes that. After supervised steps first, held-out utility is 0.34 (average of strata) and 0.33 (worst-stratum weighted) against 0.11 from scratch. Weighting the worst stratum raises the worst stratum (-0.03 against -0.24 for the average version) without lowering the mean, but the intervals are wide.

3. The biggest single gain came from the simplest lever: training longer with a faster encoder learning rate. Utility on sequences the model had trained on went from 0.56 to 0.82, on far-tier sequences from 0.45 to 0.55 (the best of any method there; nearest neighbour scores 0.31), and held-out average from 0.27 to 0.35. The first comparison of loss functions was therefore confounded by underfitting.

4. A nearest-neighbour rule is a strong baseline. It scores 0.86 on seen, 0.63 near, 0.58 mid and 0.31 far. Fine-tuning degrades more gracefully with distance (0.55 on far), so the best method depends on how far the new sequence is. A hybrid that retrieves when a close neighbour exists and uses the 200-step model otherwise tracks nearest neighbour near and mid and the model far, but does not beat nearest neighbour on the overall held-out average (0.35 against 0.40, intervals overlapping).

5. Host is learnable; region is not. Held-out host-only utility is 0.52 to 0.71 for the trained methods and nearest neighbour (0.03 for the frozen probe). Region-only utility is about 0 for every method (nearest neighbour 0.10): from one protein, none of these models can say where in the world a sequence came from any better than abstaining.

6. Optimising one stratum alone does not help that stratum and hurts the rest (warm-start budget, host head only): the model trained on one stratum scores -0.06 relative to the average model on its own stratum and -0.68 on every other stratum. The region head looks perfect on its own stratum only because region is a constant label inside a stratum, an artefact of how we defined strata. The proper-budget version of this experiment is still running.

7. The tiers hold up under a second similarity measure: 67% of sequences land in the same tier using protein-model embeddings (about 39% by chance), and nearest neighbour is again best near, the fine-tuned model best far.
8. Our own split names misled us: 'dev' (whole clusters held out) is the far tier, while 34% of test_geo rows are near-copies of training sequences.
The single-stratum transfer experiment at the proper training budget (running). Until it lands, finding 6 is for an underfit model.

Warm-start utility at the proper budget against cross-entropy at the proper budget: does tying the loss to the metric beat simply training enough? At 200 steps they are indistinguishable (0.34 against 0.35, intervals overlapping).
Repeating with another seed set and a larger encoder, and varying lambda in the utility.
The untested ideas from the scouting list: retrieval as model input, hierarchical host labels, codon tokens, better abstention rules.

items.t: The innovation loop: how new ideas get into the work
items.s: Scout, triage, test small, log the result.
p: Besides running experiments, each cycle starts with a scan for new ideas: new arXiv (q-bio, cs.LG), bioRxiv (bioinformatics, genomics, evolutionary biology) and ChemRxiv preprints, within our domain and from other fields. An idea is worth a test only if it passes four questions: is the claim checkable, does it change something we can measure here, can we test it on one GPU in a day, and what would count as it failing. Results, including failures, are logged on this page.

kids.t: Scouting pass, 2026-11-12: your suggested ideas, checked
kids.s: Verified or unverified, with sources. Search coverage was thin; nothing here is a full-text read.

head: Idea
What we found
Verdict for us
rows: Marin 1B as a base model
No model named Marin 1B found. The only roughly 1B Marin checkpoint is a general text language model; Marin-8B is Apache-2.0.
Not relevant to sequences. Dropped.
AlphaGenome (and an 'AlphaGenome 2')

A human regulatory-genome model: predicts expression, splicing, chromatin and contacts from up to 1 Mb of DNA. Nature 2026-01-28. Weights non-commercial; needs a large GPU. No virus support documented. No 'AlphaGenome 2' found.
Not usable for viral host or place. Successor UNVERIFIED.
JEPA-style model

JEPA-DNA (arXiv 2602.17162, Feb 2026) adds a latent-prediction loss to a DNA language model; a single-cell JEPA exists. No protein-sequence JEPA found. A 100M NVIDIA checkpoint is UNVERIFIED (licence and release status unclear).
Interesting auxiliary loss, but DNA-only. Deprioritised.
Fine-tune Evo 2 on viruses

Evo 2 excluded eukaryotic viruses from training. One preprint fine-tuned the 7B on 110 viral genomes: lower perplexity on unseen viruses, AUROC 0.6 for SARS-CoV-2 escape. Hardware needs on a V100 UNVERIFIED.
Possible but weak signal and heavy. Deprioritised.
Nucleotide Transformer v3 (8M to 650M)
DNA models trained on 24 animal and plant species; no viral training data mentioned. Non-commercial licence.
Viral coverage UNVERIFIED.
ESM C (300M, 600M)
Strong small protein models with a fine-tuning-friendly licence (terms for 600M UNVERIFIED; the HF card shows conflicting licence tags).
Best candidate for a stronger encoder.
Codon-level tokens
Mixed evidence: CaLM beat larger protein models on some tasks, while a later comparison found amino-acid models ahead.
Cheap to try; synonymous changes may carry lineage signal.
Retrieval of training homologs as input
RAG-ESM (ICLR 2025) and Profluent's E1 (Nov 2025) feed homologs to the model. Not shown for classification.
Fits our held-out geography and time splits. Our own nearest-neighbour baseline already beats the fine-tuned model.
Hierarchical host labels
HAVEN (bioRxiv, Jun 2025) predicts host at several taxonomic ranks. Page could not be read in full.
Cheap multi-rank heads. Benefit UNVERIFIED.
Augmentation by deliberate perturbation
Codon-degeneracy and other augmentations exist; reported gains are on small or imbalanced data. No evidence found that they help out-of-distribution.
Test as a hypothesis, do not assume.
Overlap-controlled evaluation
Two 2026 papers show pretrained-model gains can shrink or vanish on strict no-overlap tiers: both argue for tiered tests.
Matches what we found: our split names did not measure difficulty.
Better abstention
Likelihood-ratio selectors for shift (ICLR 2026), a rank-based risk-coverage reward (RLSR, Jul 2026), a selective-prediction loss (SYNC, Feb 2026).
Near-zero cost on our encoder; worth testing.

kids.t: What we will try, in order
list: 1. Tiered evaluation with a second similarity measure (protein-model embeddings) to check the tiers are not an artefact of 5-mer counting.
2. A longer, faster-learning-rate fine-tune (the model is underfit).
3. A retrieval hybrid: use the nearest training sequence when it is close, the model when it is not.
4. A stronger encoder (ESM-2 150M now; ESM C if the licence is clean).
5. Better abstention rules on the existing models.
Anything from the list marked UNVERIFIED stays untested until a primary source is read.
No new architecture or loss paper from the last 90 days on selective prediction turned up (the closest are from February and July 2026). That is UNVERIFIED, not proof of absence: the search was thin.
Nothing on ProtT5 or Caduceus was checked.
One small model (35M parameters) and three viruses. A bigger model or other viruses could behave differently.
Strata sizes are uneven and some held-out strata are small, so differences between neighbouring conditions are often inside the confidence interval.
The label set is gold by internal consistency, not by outside verification.
Utility depends on lambda = 1, which we did not vary.
Held-out data comes from the same public database as the training data, so shared biases (who sequences what) are shared by both.
Nothing here says a model is safe or good for biosecurity use; it measures one narrow classification task.
